content:
@David Turturean and I are happy to announce an explicit presentation for the absolute Galois group of of Q2\mathbb{Q}_2Q2​, with four generators and two relations.  Details are available on our project website. This solves a 44-year-old problem I submitted to Epoch AI's open-problems list last winter. Of particular interest to this community:

  1. We have two separate sorry-free formalizations in Lean. I'll focus below on the one that I did (using Claude Fable 5 and Opus 4.8); David did the other using GPT 5.5 and Fable.
  2. That formalization depends on 9 results from the mathematical literature (e.g. local reciprocity for Q2\mathbb{Q}_2Q2​, local Tate duality) that we have not yet formalized (#print axioms shows these 9 plus the standard 3). If anyone knows of existing places where these results have been formalized, or if you want to help formalize them, please let us know (we will likely work on reducing this number in the coming months). Note that the version of Mathlib is pinned to a June 12 commit, so we did not use the recent work on continuous cohomology. We are happy to work on updating to a more recent version of Mathlib once the interface for continuous cohomology has stabilized.
  3. See our formalization.yaml for details (we follow the v0.3 standard). We have also set it up with the lean comparator; see our reproducibility page for detailed instructions.
  4. We made heavy use of AI at all stages of the project. The presentations were found using Fable 5 and GPT; the proof was written using GPT-5.5-Pro (apparently a stealth 5.6; see David's account on the development page); the formalizations were built by Claude and GPT agents with human orchestration; and Fable did most of the website and paper revision. See our development page for more details.

  5. After using AI so heavily in the first two parts of the project, I wanted to experiment with an AI-centered paper-writing process. I've tried to build this process into a separate project, PaperForge. The hope is that AI-written mathematics papers can be more readable than human ones eventually. Here are some ways that I think AI-written papers can add value for readers and authors.

    • One of the main benefits for authors is that the writing process can be faster since much of it is delegated to AI. Of course, this is true with AI slop as well. But the flip side is that if an author is willing to put in some work, AI can quickly build usability features that would be very annoying to do manually.
    • One such feature is differing levels of detail in exposition. PDF papers need to pick a target audience and stick with it; inspired by LMFDB knowls we've added expandable detail levels, allowing the paper to contain more detail on arguments that the reader can choose to expand or bypass.
    • Another is notation tooltips. Instead of having a big table of notation that you have to refer to, you can just hover over the symbol and see a popup with the definition (and a link to the location it was defined). This also applies for background material: an appendix summarizes background material, and whenever these terms appear there is a popup with a short explanation and link for more information.
    • The presence of a formalization also anchors AI writing, reducing the risk of hallucinated claims or citations. Having formalization show up inline as you read the paper is hopefully useful.
    • For more details see the PaperForge repo. It's still very preliminary (it's only been used on one project so far) but I'm happy to get feedback and welcome PRs.

David Roe said:

  • inspired by LMFDB knowls we've added expandable detail levels, allowing the paper to contain more detail on arguments that the reader can choose to expand or bypass.

Woah this interactive paper is super neat. Did you set this up using Verso or is this all just HTML?

David Roe said:

  1. That formalization depends on 9 results from the mathematical literature (e.g. local reciprocity for Q2\mathbb{Q}_2Q2​, local Tate duality) that we have not yet formalized (#print axioms shows these 9 plus the standard 3). If anyone knows of existing places where these results have been formalized, or if you want to help formalize them, please let us know (we will likely work on reducing this number in the coming months).

I think "reducing the number of axioms" is less important to me than "simplify the axioms to things that are easy to check". I would prefer more axioms if each one individually can be checked by humans. Ideally you want to get them down to something that can be stated with only the definitions in Mathlib (or a few small defs). I noticed your challenge.lean file imports the axiom file explicitly, along with a few others:

import GQ2.GammaA
import GQ2.Roe.GammaR
import GQ2.Foundations.Axioms

The Foundation.Axioms file similarly imports a ton of other files which makes it really hard to audit. As an example, one of your axioms "The relative Stiefel–Whitney identity" is quite complicated and relies on several custom definitions. Maybe somebody with a stronger math background can check that this is stated correctly, but I personally find it impenetrable:

axiom GQ2.relativeStiefelWhitney_dyadic (k : IntermediateField ℚ_[2] (AlgebraicClosure ℚ_[2])) [FiniteDimensional ℚ_[2] ↥k] (d : (↥k)ˣ) (δ β : AlgebraicClosure ℚ_[2]) (hδ : δ ^ 2 = ↑↑d) (hdeg : Module.finrank ↥k ↥(quadExt k δ) = 2) (a : (↥(quadExt k δ))ˣ) (hβ : β ^ 2 = ↑↑a) (hβ0 : β ≠ 0) (hidx : ((MulAction.stabilizer (Kummer.GaloisGroup ℚ_[2]) δ).subgroupOf k.fixingSubgroup).index = 2) (s : ↥k.fixingSubgroup) (hs : s ∉ (MulAction.stabilizer (Kummer.GaloisGroup ℚ_[2]) δ).subgroupOf k.fixingSubgroup) (htriv : ∀ (g : ↥k.fixingSubgroup) (m : ZMod 2), g • m = m) (hUo : IsOpen ↑((MulAction.stabilizer (Kummer.GaloisGroup ℚ_[2]) δ).subgroupOf k.fixingSubgroup)) (α : ↥((MulAction.stabilizer (Kummer.GaloisGroup ℚ_[2]) δ).subgroupOf k.fixingSubgroup) → ZMod 2) (hαdef :
  ∀ (g : ↥((MulAction.stabilizer (Kummer.GaloisGroup ℚ_[2]) δ).subgroupOf k.fixingSubgroup)),
    α g = Kummer.kummerCocycleFun β ↑↑g) (hα :
  ∀ (g h : ↥((MulAction.stabilizer (Kummer.GaloisGroup ℚ_[2]) δ).subgroupOf k.fixingSubgroup)), α (g * h) = α g + α h) (hαc : Continuous α) :
swOne k (traceFormTwisted k δ ↑a) = swOne k (traceFormOne k δ) + corH1 htriv hUo hidx hs α hα hαc ∧   swTwo k htriv (traceFormTwisted k δ ↑a) =     swTwo k htriv (traceFormOne k δ) +         ((trivialCupPairing 2 (↥k.fixingSubgroup) htriv) (swOne k (traceFormOne k δ)))
          (corH1 htriv hUo hidx hs α hα hαc) +       evensNormH2 htriv hUo hidx hs α hα hαc

There are a few things that I've improved along these lines today based on your feedback:

  • Challenge.lean no longer imports the axiom file at all; the axioms are only needed for the solution.
  • GQ2/Foundations/Axioms.lean now contains the nine axiom declarations and nothing else; the former-axioms-now-theorems have been moved.
  • axiom-closure.md is an autogenerated file recording the dependencies for each axiom, in terms of project definitions and literature theorems. The union across all nine is 115 definitions + 12 referenced theorem statements.

I'll also note that the Lean-Compass report, `atlas-audit.md' reduces the capstone's 1,789-node dependency closure to a 30-declaration semantic review cone. Still a lot....

Unfortunately, the theorems underlying these nine results are not simple mathematics (which is why I didn't just formalize them). I think the right approach is to start a push to incorporate them into #Tau Ceti, but that will take a little while.
Congrats to both of you! What I am more in awe is the whole paper forge and this interactive paper that you all wrote as well and the development page :)!
